🚀South Lebanon: The Count Kept Rising

At 5:30 a.m., Lebanese media reported intensive Israeli strikes in the south. A minute later came word of casualties. Then the arithmetic began.

One dead. Several wounded. Then seven dead and two wounded. Then seven and three.

By morning, an Israeli strike had destroyed a home on the outskirts of Ansar, near Nabatieh. Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency reported seven killed. The Health Ministry said the dead included three children and two women. The Israeli military said it had struck Hezbollah infrastructure. 

That gap is the war in miniature. Israel sees infrastructure. Lebanon counts people pulled from the ruins of a house.

The attack followed a Friday speech by Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem, who described the June 26 U.S.-mediated framework agreement as “an Israeli order written in Israeli ink” that Lebanon’s authorities had signed. He urged them to reverse what he called a “sinful” mistake. Reuters reported the quote from Qassem’s speech. 

But neither the timing nor the rhetoric establishes why the strike happened. Israel says only that Hezbollah acted against its soldiers near the Ali Taher ridge, without describing what occurred. The military cited that action as the reason for strikes on both Ali Taher and Ansar. The ridge is about six miles from the Israeli border and has become a recurrent flashpoint. 

Elsewhere: artillery fire near Ali Taher and Wadi al-Hujeir; controlled demolitions in Hadatha and Zawtar; fighter-jet strikes near Nabatieh al-Fawqa; small-arms fire in Aita al-Jabal; and later attacks near Aitaroun, Tyre, Mays al-Jabal and al-Mansouri.

A later strike on Deir al-Zahrani initially left two dead and nine wounded, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry. The ministry later revised the toll there to four dead, bringing the day’s reported total to at least 11 killed. The New York Times reported nine deaths at an earlier point in the day; other reports later cited 11. 

Prime Minister Nawaf Salam described the escalation as “extremely dangerous.” He said the people killed in Ansar were not “military infrastructure,” and that women and children were not military targets. 

The June 26 framework agreement was supposed to exchange an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon for Hezbollah’s disarmament and a wider Lebanese Army deployment. Israel says it will maintain its positions until Hezbollah disarms. 

Hezbollah calls the arrangement surrender.

🇺🇸⚔️🇮🇷 The New York Times reports that the USS Abraham Lincoln's supply crisis traces back to Iran's opening strikes on the war's first days, when Iranian missiles and attack drones heavily damaged the U.S. Navy base in Bahrain, the fleet's main logistics hub in the region for decades.

With that hub destroyed and other regional ports like Fujairah also within Iranian missile range, the Pentagon shifted its supply chain to the British-run base on Diego Garcia, 2,200 miles from where the Lincoln and a second carrier strike group operate in the Gulf of Oman. Then-UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer initially denied the Pentagon access to Diego Garcia, only relenting on March 1 for what he called a "specific and limited defensive purpose." Iran later fired two medium-range ballistic missiles at the island; one fell short into the Indian Ocean and a U.S. warship intercepted the other.

The Lincoln has now spent nearly nine months at sea without a single liberty port, well past the point where its crew would be eligible for five "beer days" under Navy tradition. Trump dismissed Democratic senators' concerns about the deployment on Friday, saying the ship is being replaced by the USS George Washington, and separately said the deployment was "not nearly long enough." 🎙 Tehran, Dushanbe explore expanded cooperation in water, electricity

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Iran and Tajikistan have explored ways to expand cooperation in water and electricity, with Iran expressing readiness to provide technical assistance for improving and developing Tajikistan’s power grid.

According to Iran’s Energy Ministry, Iran’s Energy Minister Abbas Aliabadi held talks with Tajikistan’s Minister of Energy and Water Resources Daler Juma, discussing prospects for broader economic, technical, cultural and scientific cooperation between the two countries.
​
Aliabadi highlighted the deep historical and cultural ties between Iran and Tajikistan, saying the two sides discussed future cooperation in areas including culture, tourism, science and technology, water and electricity.
​
Addressing challenges facing Tajikistan’s electricity network, Aliabadi said Iran was prepared to cooperate technically with Tajikistan to help improve and develop its power sector.
​
The Iranian minister also emphasized Tehran’s strategy of strengthening relations with neighboring countries, describing Tajikistan as a country with deep and historic links to Iran. He noted that people in some border areas of the two countries have family ties, adding that stronger cooperation with neighbors would contribute to greater regional solidarity.
​
Juma, for his part, said the meeting focused on expanding economic, commercial, technical and cultural cooperation and stressed the importance of increasing trade relations between Tajikistan and Iran.
​
The two sides also discussed shared dams, energy and logistics, cultural and information-related issues, and human-resource development in power plants.
​
In the end, Juma expressed hope that the talks would yield positive results, similar to their previous meeting.

🇭🇷 Wildfires are ripping through Croatia's Dalmatian coast, described as one of the worst outbreaks in the country's history.

A blaze near Lokva Rogoznica spread overnight toward the tourist town of Omis, driven by hurricane-force winds, forcing 1,000 to 2,000 residents and tourists to evacuate, many of them foreign nationals including around 300 Czech tourists. At least one person has died and one remains missing. Fourteen people were hospitalized, ten in intensive care.

Nearly 300 firefighters battled the blaze overnight, with reinforcements sent from Zagreb and other counties.

Homes, cafes, cars and boats were destroyed as flames reached the Borak area above the Omis town center. Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said the government is coordinating response in real time in a region hosting 12,000 tourists on top of its 15,000 residents.

The fire comes amid a broader wildfire wave hitting Croatia during a prolonged heatwave, with similar blazes forcing evacuations across Germany, France, the UK, and Greece.

🔻 Israeli forces launch air, artillery, and phosphorus attacks on southern Lebanon

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Israeli forces have launched airstrikes as well as artillery and heavy-machine-gun fire against areas in southern Lebanon’s Nabatieh district, using phosphorus shells.

Al Mayadeen network’s correspondent in southern Lebanon reported that Israeli warplanes targeted an area between Ali al-Taher and al-Dabsha in the Nabatieh district.
​
Israeli occupation forces simultaneously fired heavy machine guns at the heights of Ali al-Taher, while Israeli artillery targeted the area with phosphorus shells, Al Mayadeen reported.
​
The attacks came hours after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu threatened Lebanon and accused Hezbollah of violating the ceasefire by attacking Israeli forces inside the so-called “Yellow Line.”
​
Netanyahu claimed that the Israeli military was continuing its operations in Lebanon and the Gaza Strip in accordance with political directives.
​
He said the regime’s forces were acting to remove what he called threats from Lebanon and Gaza.
​
Hezbollah has been accused by Israel of violating the ceasefire, while Lebanon and Hezbollah have repeatedly condemned Israeli attacks and violations of the truce.
​
The latest strikes come amid continuing tensions in southern Lebanon despite the ceasefire and a framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel.
